lead: Both readings today are about a will joined to God's will. Hebrews lets us hear the Son say to the Father as he comes into the world: “See, God, I have come to do your will.” In Matthew, Jesus shows what that will looks like when someone wrongs us: no revenge, the second mile, and love even for the enemy. On this Saturday of the Apostles' Fast we also remember St Jude Thaddaeus, one of the Twelve. The key words are body, will and enemy.

r.h: See, I have come to do your will
set: The Letter to the Hebrews does not name its author. The early Church in the East received it among the letters of Paul; already in the third century Origen said that only God knows who wrote it. It is a long sermon to Christians who were tempted to grow tired and fall back. Chapters 8 to 10 compare the sacrifices of the old covenant, repeated year after year, with the one sacrifice of Christ.

Just before our passage the author says that “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (10:4). He then puts the words of Psalm 40 on the lips of Christ. He quotes the psalm in its Greek form, the Septuagint, which reads “a body you have prepared for me” where the Hebrew text has “you have given me an open ear”.
str: vv. 5–7: the Son's words as he enters the world: not sacrifices, but a body and an obedient will.
vv. 8–9: the author explains: the first order of sacrifice is taken away to establish the second.
v. 10: the result: we are made holy by the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
kw: The key to the passage. The Hebrew psalm speaks of an ear opened to obey; the Greek speaks of a body. Both point to the same thing: a whole human life given over to God. For Hebrews this body is the Incarnation itself, offered on the Cross.
God's will is not a cold decree. It is his saving plan. Christ's human will said yes to it at every moment, and in that yes we are made holy.
A favourite word of Hebrews (7:27; 9:12; 10:10). The sacrifice of Christ does not need to be repeated, because nothing is lacking to it.
vv: Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body you have prepared for me;
The prophets had already said that God wanted obedience more than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6). The old sacrifices were not bad, but they could only point beyond themselves.
See, God, I have come to do your will, O God
The whole life of Jesus is in this sentence. He says it at his coming into the world, in Nazareth, in Gethsemane (“not my will but yours be done”, Luke 22:42) and on the Cross.
He abolishes the first in order to establish the second.
The “first” is the system of animal sacrifices; the “second” is the doing of God's will by Christ. This is not contempt for Israel's worship, which God himself had given, but its fulfilment.
we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
“Have been sanctified” is a perfect tense in Greek: something done once whose effect remains. Holiness is first a gift received, before it is a task.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches the Incarnation: the Son took a body in order to offer it (CCC 462), and Christ's whole life is an offering to the Father, from his coming into the world to the Cross (CCC 606). The Church teaches that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Holy Qurbono are one single sacrifice: the victim is the same, only the manner of offering is different (CCC 1367). The Qurbono does not add a new sacrifice to the Cross. It makes the one offering present, so that we can join our own bodies and wills to it (Romans 12:1).

set: These verses belong to the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5 to 7), and to a series of six sayings in which Jesus says: “You have heard that it was said… But I say to you” (5:21–48). He has just said that he came not to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfil them (5:17). These sayings do not cancel the Law. They go to its root, the heart.

“An eye for an eye” is found in the Law of Moses (Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21). It was a rule for judges, and it set a limit: the penalty must not be greater than the injury. In later Jewish practice it was generally applied as payment of damages. Jesus does not call the old rule cruel. He asks his disciples to go beyond justice to a generosity that breaks the chain of revenge.
str: v. 38: the old rule: an eye for an eye.
vv. 39–42: four examples: the cheek, the coat, the mile, the one who asks.
vv. 43–44: the old saying about neighbour and enemy, and the new command: love and pray.
kw: Here it means to strike back, to answer evil with evil, as in a lawsuit or a fight. Paul says the same: “Do not repay anyone evil for evil” (Romans 12:17).

A word from the Persian royal post. In Jesus' day a Roman soldier could make a civilian carry his load for a mile. The same verb is used of Simon of Cyrene, “compelled” to carry the cross (Matthew 27:32).
Not a feeling of liking, which cannot be commanded, but a will to do good to the other. Jesus joins it to prayer, the first good we can do for an enemy.
vv: But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also;

To strike the right cheek, a right-handed person would use the back of the hand. Many commentators think Jesus means an insult more than an assault. The disciple does not answer the insult with another.
and if anyone wants to sue you and take your coat, give your cloak as well;

The coat was the inner tunic; the cloak was the outer garment that also served as a blanket at night. The Law protected the poor man's cloak: it had to be returned before sunset (Exodus 22:26–27). Jesus asks the disciple to give up even what the Law allowed him to keep.
and if anyone forces you to go one mile, go also the second mile.
The first mile is forced; the second is a gift. The disciple turns an act of oppression into an act of service.
But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,

The Law of Moses never commands hatred of the enemy. It commands help even for an enemy's ox or donkey (Exodus 23:4–5), and Proverbs says, “If your enemies are hungry, give them bread to eat” (Proverbs 25:21). The saying “hate your enemy” in verse 43 was probably a popular narrowing of “neighbour”. Jesus opens the commandment to everyone.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in the Sermon on the Mount Jesus forbids anger, hatred and vengeance, and asks his disciples to turn the other cheek and love their enemies (CCC 2262). It also teaches that this does not take away the right and duty of legitimate defence, above all for those responsible for the lives of others (CCC 2263–2265). Jesus himself, struck before the high priest, asked calmly, “why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). What he forbids is revenge, not the defence of the innocent. Christian prayer reaches its height in forgiving enemies (CCC 2844).

qa: Does “do not resist an evildoer” mean that Christians must let evil go unchecked?

No. Jesus speaks of personal revenge, not of the protection of the weak or the work of just authority. Paul, in the same letter where he says “do not repay evil for evil”, says that rulers are God's servants for our good (Romans 13:4). The Catechism teaches that legitimate defence can be a grave duty for one responsible for others (CCC 2265). What the Gospel asks of each of us is to refuse hatred, to forgive, and to pray for those who wrong us.
rite: Today the Panchangam remembers Mar Yuda Thaddai Shleeha. Matthew and Mark call him Thaddaeus (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18); Luke calls him Judas son of James (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). John remembers one question he asked at the Last Supper: “Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?” (John 14:22). Old traditions tell of his preaching in the East and his martyrdom, though the details are uncertain. The short Letter of Jude bears the name of “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (Jude 1); whether this is the apostle is discussed among scholars. Jude learned the lesson of today's Gospel from the Lord himself: the love that prays even for those who persecute.
study: Hebrews puts Psalm 40 on the lips of Christ: “See, God, I have come to do your will.” Where in my day does God ask me to say the same words?
Who is the person I find hardest to pray for? What would the “second mile” look like with that person this week?
